title: Fat Bear Week Returns: 16 Bears Compete for the Chubby Crown
summary:
It's that time of year again — time to vote for the chubbiest bear in Alaska. Fat Bear Week is back for its 12th year, running from September 22 to September 29, 2026. Fans worldwide can cast their votes for the fattest brown bear at Katmai National Park.

Katmai spans 4.1 million acres of volcanoes, rivers, and forests. It's home to about 2,200 brown bears that feast on salmon-rich rivers. The bears rely on these fat reserves to survive the long, harsh winter.

The contest began in 2014 when Park Ranger Mike Fitz noticed two photos of the same bear on the park's bear camera. One was taken in June, the other in September. The difference was dramatic — the bear had packed on serious pounds. Fitz and other rangers turned the idea into a one-day event called "Fat Bear Tuesday" on Facebook, where votes were counted through "likes." The next year, it expanded into a full week.

Now, it's a single-elimination competition. Each day, fans vote online for one of two bears in a matchup. The winner advances; the other is eliminated. The final round is on September 29.

This year, 16 bears and bear families are competing. Bear 32, or Chunk, is back to defend his 2025 title after recovering from a broken jaw. Bear 164, or Bucky, wowed fans by snatching leaping salmon out of the air. Bear 132 is raising three cubs — one got separated this summer and survived alone for several days before reuniting. And Bear 806 is caring for her own cub plus an adopted young bear named Biggie.

In 2025, more than 1.7 million votes were cast from over 100 countries. Whether you vote for a returning champion or a newcomer, Fat Bear Week is a fun way to celebrate these amazing animals — and a reminder to protect their wild Alaskan home.
why_it_matters: Fat Bear Week shows how a wildlife agency can turn dry biology — hibernation, salmon runs, fat reserves — into something millions of people care about, which matters because public attention is often what protects a park's budget and its rivers. It also quietly raises a bigger question for this generation: the bears' survival depends on salmon runs that warming oceans and human water use can weaken, so the contest is measuring how well the ecosystem is feeding its top predator.

background_read: Fat Bear Week is run by the U.S. National Park Service (the government agency that manages America's national parks) and grew out of the park's live bear cameras, which stream video of brown bears fishing at Brooks Falls. In 2014 a ranger named Mike Fitz compared two photos of the same bear — one from June and one from September — and the striking difference turned into a one-day Facebook poll called Fat Bear Tuesday before expanding into a full week.

Katmai National Park and Preserve (a 4.1-million-acre park in southwest Alaska, full of volcanoes, rivers and brown bears) protects a landscape reshaped by the colossal Novarupta volcanic eruption of 1912, one of the largest eruptions of the 20th century. Every summer its rivers fill with sockeye salmon swimming upstream to spawn, and the bears gather at falls and rapids to catch them, sometimes snatching fish out of the air.

A single-elimination bracket works much like the March Madness college basketball tournament: lose once and you are out, so fans vote in a series of head-to-head matchups until one bear remains. The timing is not random — the contest ends in late September and early October, just before the bears den for the winter, when a brown bear stops eating and drinking for months and lives entirely off the fat it stored.

The contest has become a model for reaching people who will never visit Alaska: a famous older bear named Otis won the title several times, and votes now arrive from more than 100 countries. Biologists point out that the bears' fat is only as reliable as the salmon runs that supply it, and those runs are affected by warming oceans, dams and fishing pressure far from the park.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — fans, the park and local communities
perspectives.description: The contest turns a remote Alaska park into a worldwide talking point and gives people who will never see a brown bear a reason to learn how salmon rivers work. More than 1.7 million votes from over 100 countries show how far a simple, joyful idea can travel, and the attention supports tourism and support for protecting Katmai.

Some critics argue that crowning the chubbiest bear turns a survival story into a cute internet game, focusing on memes and nicknames instead of the real threats: shrinking salmon runs, warming oceans and pressure on rivers. A voting bracket does not by itself protect habitat, and treating wild animals as characters can blur the line between conservation and entertainment.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a pattern of citizen science
perspectives.description: Fat Bear Week fits a long tradition of projects that use the public's eyes to gather and discuss real wildlife data, like bird counts where volunteers log the species they see. The bracket is also a genuine biological measure: arriving just before winter denning, a bear's size is essentially a scoreboard for how well it and its river have done that year.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what the contest may reveal next
perspectives.description: If salmon runs keep changing, future Fat Bear Weeks may become an annual snapshot of which rivers and which bears are coping best, useful information for park managers and biologists. The same audience could also be asked to support salmon habitat, making the fun contest a starting point rather than the finish line.
